blocks.text: 1. Model Serialization

blocks.alt: A trained model is serialized into a saved file

blocks.text: The Multimodal Deep Learning module, already covered across this course, focused purely on model architecture. Model Serialization, saving a trained model's own weights and structure to disk, addresses what happens right after training finishes.
This topic genuinely opens this course's own Production Deep Learning module, the foundation every other topic in this module builds on.
2. Why Training Happens Separately From Deployment
This connects back to training, already covered generally across this course. Training genuinely happens once, often on genuinely powerful, dedicated hardware.
Deployment genuinely happens repeatedly, often on genuinely different, more constrained hardware later on, a genuinely important separation explored throughout the rest of this topic.
3. Weights And Architecture Together

blocks.alt: Weights and architecture are saved together

blocks.text: This connects back to why training happens separately from deployment, already covered in this topic. A genuinely saved model file must genuinely capture both the trained weight values and the network's own architecture.
Genuinely missing either piece leaves the saved file genuinely unusable for real inference, the exact two-part requirement explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 4. Framework Specific Formats

blocks.alt: PyTorch uses .pt while TensorFlow uses SavedModel

blocks.text: This connects back to weights and architecture together, already covered in this topic. Each genuinely deep learning framework genuinely defines its own native file format for saving models.
This genuinely tightly couples a saved model to the exact framework that originally trained it, a genuinely real practical limitation explored throughout the rest of this topic.
5. Serialization Versus Checkpointing

blocks.alt: Serialization saves the final model while checkpointing saves a training snapshot

blocks.text: This connects back to framework specific formats, already covered in this topic. A genuinely training checkpoint typically also saves optimizer state, letting training genuinely resume later.
A genuinely final, deployed serialization usually only genuinely needs the weights themselves, nothing more, a genuinely useful, practical distinction explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This distinction, already covered in this topic, directly explains why deployed model files are often genuinely much smaller than the full training checkpoints they were originally saved from during training.

blocks.text: 6. Version Compatibility Risks

blocks.alt: An old framework version is compared against a new framework version

blocks.text: This connects back to serialization versus checkpointing, already covered in this topic. A genuinely saved model file genuinely depends on the exact library version that originally created it.
Genuinely loading it with a mismatched, incompatible version can genuinely fail or silently misbehave, a genuinely real, practical risk explored throughout the rest of this topic.
7. Preview Of Cross Framework Portability

blocks.alt: A PyTorch model goes through ONNX to reach another runtime

blocks.text: This connects back to version compatibility risks, already covered in this topic. Genuinely framework-specific formats create a genuinely real portability problem across different deployment environments.
ONNX, covered as the next topic in this module, genuinely exists specifically to solve exactly that portability problem, a genuinely direct motivation explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This portability motivation, already covered in this topic, directly sets up ONNX, covered as the next topic in this module, as a genuinely direct solution to the framework coupling already covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: 8. Serialized Model Size Considerations
This connects back to cross-framework portability preview, already covered in this topic. A genuinely large model's own serialized file can genuinely reach many gigabytes in raw size.
Already covered generally as quantization in Quantization, one genuinely direct way to shrink that saved file, a genuinely practical technique already familiar from earlier in this course.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Model serialization saves a trained model's own weights and structure to disk.
Training happens once on powerful hardware; deployment happens repeatedly on different hardware.
A saved model file must capture both the trained weights and the network's own architecture.
Each deep learning framework defines its own native file format, tightly coupling models to it.
Training checkpoints save optimizer state too; final deployed serialization usually needs only weights.
A saved model file depends on the exact library version that created it, risking compatibility issues.
Framework-specific formats create a real portability problem across deployment environments.
Large models can produce serialized files reaching many gigabytes; quantization helps shrink them.
Next up: ONNX, a format solving the cross-framework portability problem directly.
